query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under service-relevant thermal and mechanical conditions, an ostensibly single-phase high-entropy alloy can undergo a low-temperature, thermally activated phase decomposition that generates nanoscale brittle intermetallic precipitates—especially near grain boundaries—which act as stress concentrators and promote decohesion, thereby leading to emergent brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., an ordered B2 HEA such as AlCoFeNi) with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to a controlled thermal treatment (prolonged annealing at an intermediate temperature favorable for decomposition) versus a rapid cooling process to preserve the single-phase state.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant temperature ranges and strain rates, with the annealing treatment mimicking long-term or cyclic thermal exposures encountered in demanding engineering applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale brittle intermetallic precipitates that form along or near the grain boundaries within the otherwise ductile matrix.
generation.mechanism: The controlled annealing triggers a thermally activated spinodal or nucleation-driven phase separation within the single-phase HEA. The resulting fine precipitates, due to their inherent brittleness and incoherent interfaces with the matrix, serve as localized crack initiation sites when the alloy is mechanically loaded.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the rapidly cooled, homogeneous baseline, the annealed specimen will exhibit a significant reduction in overall toughness, displaying earlier crack initiation and brittle fracture during tensile testing.
generation.baseline: A fast-cooled HEA sample that retains its homogeneous, single-phase microstructure with high toughness under similar testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under long-term or cyclic thermal exposures and moderate to high mechanical loading conditions typical of demanding service environments. The precise temperature window and time scale for the onset of decomposition remain to be fully defined.
generation.uncertainty: Key uncertainties include the exact thermal threshold and kinetics for the phase decomposition, the size and distribution of brittle precipitates required to cause a measurable loss of toughness, and the influence of alloy composition variations on these phenomena.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA specimens. One set is subjected to a prolonged annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (close to the expected onset of decomposition) to intentionally promote nanoscale phase separation; the other set is rapidly cooled to maintain a homogeneous microstructure. Conduct identical tensile tests on both sets while performing detailed microstructural analyses using TEM and EBSD both before and after mechanical loading.
measurements: Detection and mapping of any nanoscale precipitates (phase decomposition) using TEM/EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed specimens do not show a significant increase in the presence of brittle precipitates (particularly near grain boundaries) or if their toughness does not decrease relative to the fast-cooled baseline (i.e., no correlation between induced phase decomposition and brittle fracture is observed), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.
